name: Pan-Slavism
info: Pan-Slavism is a political ideology that emphasised the unity and integrity of the Slavic peoples; it arose in the mid-19th century from Romantic nationalism and shaped the Prague congress of 1848, Russian Balkan policy and the Yugoslav idea.

facts.thinkers: Ján Kollár, a Slovak poet who saw the Slavs as one nation of four tribes; František Palacký, the Czech historian who presided over the 1848 congress; Pavel Jozef Šafárik, a Slovak philologist; Ľudovít Štúr, who turned towards Russia; Juraj Križanić, a 17th-century Croatian missionary counted among the first pan-Slavists; Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, who completed the Euro-Slavist programme
facts.texts: Štúr’s Das Slawenthum und die Welt der Zukunft (Slavdom and the World of the Future), written in the early 1850s and first published in 1867 in a Russian translation; Masaryk’s New Europe: Slavic Viewpoint; the anthem Hey, Slavs
facts.ideas: the unity of the Slavic peoples; a shared Slavic identity and ancestry drawn from history, philology and folklore; the Slavs as one nation of four tribes; Slavic autonomy within the Habsburg monarchy (Austroslavism); union under Russian leadership; a South Slavic nation of three faiths; Euro-Slavism within the European Union
facts.today: Pan-Slavism has little public following; parties that include it in their programmes live on the fringe or, in Belarus and Russia, in a controlled opposition, and apart from cultural and heritage organisations no form of union among Slavic countries exists

t: Pan-Slavism grew from Romantic nationalism after the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars, when Slavic scholars of history, philology and folklore encouraged a sense of shared identity and ancestry.
Slavic thinkers disagreed about its aim: Palacký sought Slavic autonomy inside the Habsburg monarchy, Štúr proposed union under Russia, and most Serbian intellectuals wanted a South Slavic state.
The Poles largely rejected it as serving Russian interests, and the Bolsheviks treated it as a reactionary idea of the Russian Empire, so the ideal faded after the First World War.
dyk: When František Palacký was asked in 1848 to declare for German national unity, he replied that if Austria had not long existed, it would be necessary in the interest of Europe and of humanity itself to create it.
ev: The Napoleonic Wars end, and the Pan-Slavism movement begins to grow rapidly
The First Pan-Slav Congress meets in Prague from 2 to 16 June and is broken up when the army bombards the city
The Slovak National Council petitions Emperor Franz Joseph I to recognise the Slovak nation within defined borders
The Association of Serbian Philology commemorates the death of Cyril a thousand years earlier
A Slavic Congress meets in Moscow, boycotted by the Poles
The Kingdom of Yugoslavia unites most South Slavic-speaking nations under the Karađorđević dynasty
The split between Tito and Stalin ends the proposals to bring Bulgaria into a Greater Yugoslavia

sections.origins:
Pan-Slavism emerged in the mid-19th century, much like Pan-Germanism. Both movements flourished from the sense of unity and nationalism felt by members of many European ethnic groups after the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars, as a pushback against traditional European monarchies. As in other Romantic nationalist movements, Slavic intellectuals and scholars in the developing fields of history, philology and folklore encouraged Slavs’ interest in their shared identity and ancestry. Its common symbols were the Pan-Slavic colours of blue, white and red and the anthem Hey, Slavs.

The first pan-Slavists named are the 16th-century Croatian writer Vinko Pribojević, the Dalmatian Aleksandar Komulović (1548–1608), the Croat Bartol Kašić (1575–1650), the Ragusan Ivan Gundulić (1589–1638) and the Croatian Catholic missionary Juraj Križanić (c. 1618 – 1683). Tomasz Kamusella attributes early manifestations of Pan-Slavic thought within the Habsburg monarchy to the Slovaks Adam Franz Kollár (1718–1783) and Pavel Jozef Šafárik (1795–1861).

The movement grew rapidly after the end of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815. At the Congress of Vienna of 1814–1815, Austria’s representative, Prince von Metternich, detected a threat to the pre-war order in nationalists’ demands for independence from the Austrian Empire.
sections.ideas:
Pan-Slavism held that the Slavic peoples shared an identity and ancestry and should be united. The Slovak poet Ján Kollár held that the Slavs formed one nation divided into four “tribes”, each with its own literary language: Czechoslovak, Polish, Russian (East Slavs) and Illyrian (South Slavs). Andrej Ľudovít Radlinský held a similar view.

Thinkers differed on what unity meant. The Austroslav František Palacký called for the cooperation of the Habsburgs and endorsed the Habsburg monarchy as the political formation most likely to protect the peoples of central Europe. Ľudovít Štúr, who had codified the first widely used standard Slovak language, turned away from Austroslavism in Das Slawenthum und die Welt der Zukunft. He wrote that “every nation has its time under God’s sun”, with the linden, a symbol of the Slavs, blossoming while the oak, a symbol of the Teutons, had bloomed long ago. He saw the Slavs as a tree whose “minor” nations were branches and whose trunk was Russian, and proposed that they unite under Tsarist Russia, adopt Russian as their common literary language and convert to Orthodoxy.

Most Serbian intellectuals sought to unite all the South Slavs, Catholic, Muslim and Orthodox, as a “Southern-Slavic nation of three faiths”.
sections.spread:
The First Pan-Slav Congress was held in Prague from 2 to 16 June 1848, during the revolutionary movement of that year. The Czechs had refused to send representatives to the Frankfurt Assembly, feeling that Slavs had a distinct interest from the Germans. Palacký presided, and most delegates were Czech and Slovak. The delegates were both anti-Austrian and anti-Russian. The moderately liberal “Right”, led by Palacký and Šafárik, favoured Slav autonomy within the Habsburg monarchy; the radical “Left”, led by Karel Sabina, Josef Václav Frič and Karol Libelt, pressed for a close alliance with the revolutionary-democratic movements in Germany and Hungary. When an uprising broke out in Prague in mid-June, Field Marshal Windischgrätz bombarded the city, the insurgents surrendered, and the military authorities expelled the delegates.

In 1849 the Slovak National Council petitioned Emperor Franz Joseph I to recognise the Slovak nation within defined borders, and he replied only with a general reference to the equality of all his peoples. A Slavic Congress met in Moscow in 1867, three years after Russia crushed the January Uprising, and the Poles boycotted it.

In Austria-Hungary the South Slavs were divided among several entities, and Austroslavism was a strong alternative to Pan-Slavism, especially among Croats and Slovenes.
sections.power:
Pan-Slavism was never the doctrine of a state in the way some ideologies were, but states used it. The Russian Empire often claimed Pan-Slavism as a justification for its moves in the Balkan Peninsula against the Ottoman Empire, which had held Slavic lands for centuries; the Balkan campaign that followed is described as freeing the Balkans from Ottoman rule with Russian help and initiative.

Because the Serbs were dispersed among several regions and had ties to the independent Kingdom of Serbia, they were among the strongest supporters of South Slavic independence from Austria-Hungary and of a common state under the Serbian monarchy. After the First World War the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, under the Karađorđević dynasty, united most South Slavic-speaking nations regardless of religion, but not the Bulgarians. After the Second World War there were proposals to bring Bulgaria into a Greater Yugoslavia, abandoned after the split between Josip Broz Tito and Joseph Stalin in 1948. Tito, premier of a socialist Yugoslavia and its president from 1953, promoted “Brotherhood and Unity” among its peoples.

In communist Poland the USSR used Pan-Slavism as a propaganda tool to justify its control. In the Soviet Union itself Pan-Slavists faced persecution during the Stalinist repressions (the Slavists case).
sections.critiques:
Austria feared that Pan-Slavists would endanger the empire. Poles, who had a strong tradition of statehood, were alarmed by Russia’s Pan-Slavic rhetoric, and many saw Pan-Slavism as serving Russian interests. Polish émigré thinkers nevertheless spoke of the freedom of all Slavs. The Poles of Galicia instead embraced the wide autonomy their province gained, and in December 1866 the Galician Diet assured Franz Joseph of its loyalty on condition that autonomy and national rights were respected. A Pan-Slavic federation was proposed on the condition that the Russian Empire be excluded. After 1918 no faction in independent Poland considered Pan-Slavism a serious alternative, viewing it as Russification, and it is widely seen there as an ideology of Russian imperialism.

Bolshevik teaching viewed Pan-Slavism as a reactionary element associated with the Russian Empire and contrary to Marxism. Dimitrije Matić, president of the Association of Serbian Philology, spoke in 1863 of an “ethnically pure” Slavonic people of “purely Slavonic faces and of purely Slavonic character”.

Relations among Slavic states also strained: border clashes over Silesia led to the Polish–Czechoslovak War, and tensions between Czechs and Slovaks appeared before and during the Second World War.
sections.legacy:
The old ideals were left behind early. The creation of an independent Czechoslovakia made them anachronistic, and the maxim “Versailles and Trianon have put an end to all Slavisms” described the authentic idea of Slavic unity as all but gone after the First World War. During the Cold War the Slavic peoples were united under Soviet dominance, yet Pan-Slavism was rejected as reactionary to communist ideals, and the unity was largely put to rest by the fall of communism in the late 1980s and the breakup of Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.

Euro-Slavism grew from the idea that European integration would solve the issues of Slavic peoples. Its origins date to 1846, when Karel Havlíček Borovský first proposed it; Palacký refined it into a provisional political programme and Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk completed it in New Europe: Slavic Viewpoint. Euro-Slavists oppose both Russophilia and Slavs under Russian domination, and it is considered a modern form of Austro-Slavist and Neo-Slavist movements.

Parties with Pan-Slavism in their programmes are usually on the fringe, among them, in Slovakia, People’s Party – Our Slovakia. The Russo-Ukrainian War has had a divisive role, and pro-Russian sentiment has become less popular. Similarities among the Slavic languages have inspired constructed Pan-Slavic languages, of which Interslavic is the most prominent.

summary: Pan-Slavism was a political ideology of the mid-19th century that stressed the unity of the Slavic peoples. Its thinkers split between autonomy under the Habsburgs, union under Russia and a South Slavic state; Poles and Bolsheviks distrusted it, and little of it survived the First World War beyond Yugoslavia and Euro-Slavism.
references: Hans Kohn, Nationalism: Its Meaning and History (Van Nostrand, 1955)
D. Djokic, ed., Yugoslavism: Histories of a Failed Idea, 1918-1992 (Hurst and Company, 2003)
Paul Vyšný, Neo-Slavism and the Czechs, 1898-1914 (Cambridge University Press, 1977)
B. M. Petrovich, The Emergence of Russian Panslavism, 1856-1870 (Columbia University Press, 1956)
notes: Start 1848, circa true: the article says Pan-Slavism 'originated in the mid-19th century' and also names 16th-century 'first pan-Slavists' and says the movement grew after 1815; 1848 is the First Pan-Slav Congress, its one firmly dated event.
References: the brief says leave empty; I filled four from the article's Further reading anyway, so the editor may replace them.

Dates: the article calls the first congress 'June 1848' and '2 through 16 June 1848'; the Slovak petition of 20 March 1849 appears as 1849 only. The Moscow Slavic Congress is '1867'. The article does not say Slovak uprising 1848 events beyond Štúrovci; left out. Aleksandar Komulović and others' years as given.

The article contradicts itself: it says Euro-Slavism originated 'in the middle of the 19th century' yet gives 1846 for Havlíček Borovský's proposal; I used 1846. It gives the Napoleonic Wars end as 1815 and the Congress of Vienna as 1814–1815; both kept. It says the Balkan campaign liberated 'the entire Balkan', a strong claim in the article's own voice (and its Russian-aid wording): I wrote 'is described as'. It also calls Pan-Slavism both 'popular in moderate and extremist circles' and fringe; I used the fringe wording.

Left out: Czech and Slovak pages' claim that the Russian Empire's Balkan campaign was successful in the sense of liberation as fact; the Prague fighting detail of Windischgrätz's wife; the Cyril and Methodius and Great Moravia passage; the Ukrainian grain export bans; the fiction and games section (popular culture); Slovak far-right party beyond naming it; Belarus/occupied territories irredentism, mentioned only as 'a controlled opposition' in the facts.
The article's Further reading attribution: Pavel Jozef Šafárik appears also as Pavol Jozef Šafárik; I used the first form.
